newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SHOPKEEPERS GRUMBLE AS FANS STAY HOME.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SHOPKEEPERS GRUMBLE AS FANS STAY HOME.

text.p: The weather is superb, the pistes are in great shape and host nation Italy have already won a gold at the Alpine skiing world championships.
Only one thing is missing -- the fans.
At the opening men's super-G on Monday and the women's slalom on Wednesday, the number of spectators watching in the stands was way below expectations.
Shopkeepers in the north-western Italian resort, which has a high percentage of self-catering apartments, have begun complaining that business is suffering.

"There's not been a tourist around since Sunday evening, just athletes, officials and you journalists. You've already got everything and what you don't have the sponsors give you," lamented one resident earlier in the week.
One newspaper carried the headline "It's an economic disaster for all the shopkeepers."
Some residents have collected signatures asking for stringent traffic regulations, which limit access to Sestriere by car, to be relaxed to bring the crowds back.
Others took a more long-term view, saying they never expected a booming trade during the championships but had high hopes of reaping the rewards in future.
Gian Franco Kasper, the secretary general of the International Ski Federation (FIS) said he had been a little disappointed by the turnout so far.
"First of all the Italians concentrate more or less on (Alberto) Tomba, that we know," he said.
"But still for last night for the ladies we would have expected a little bit more."
Double world and triple Olympic champion Tomba does not race here until next week but a large crowd was expected for compatriot Deborah Compagnoni who won the slalom.
Instead, the stands were mostly full of other athletes, team officials, sponsors and volunteers.

Kasper said that "one of the mistakes" was too strict traffic regulations. "People have been informed it takes you at least two hours from the moment you are at the parking until you can get to the race.
"If it's going on like this I think we have to open the streets or at least make it a little easier."
He suggested that organisers should also have invited schools for free, particularly on a day such as Thursday when the men's combined was being held.
Television ratings were very high, Kasper said but "something is missing if you stand in the finish area."
"I think we will speak a little differently after the last Saturday night," he added, referring to the men's slalom which closes the championships with Tomba.
Few skiers seemed concerned by the lack of a crowd at the finish, most saying they were delighted the fine weather had held up and praising Italian hospitality.
"It's great, I think the weather really makes it," said Canadian Ed Podivinsky. "The Italians really know how to put on a fun show and have a good time. The snow's the best I've skied on all year."
